description: Measuresing astronauts mental health and sleep cycle. Also providing mental support if needed
summary: ASTRO is a software solution that supports astronauts' psychological well-being during long, isolated space missions. NASA reports show astronauts historically sleep about six hours a night in space, and recent ISS crews average 7.3 hours, still below their 7.9-hour preflight baseline. Lost sleep can weaken performance and health, yet NASA's evidence report notes that no study has systematically examined individual differences in sleep or circadian outcomes. ASTRO addresses this gap by combining validated psychological scales (anxiety, depression, emotional regulation, overall well-being) with sleep-cycle tracking (duration, efficiency, awakenings) into one clear well-being indicator, compared against each astronaut's personal baseline. A home dashboard shows current status at a glance, and warning signals trigger alerts and, with consent, a connection to a psychologist on Earth. Anonymized data can also help scientists understand mental health on long missions. ASTRO builds on NASA's Standard Measures and supports, not replaces, flight surgeons and psychologists. It matters because on missions to Mars, a small change in one person's mental state can affect the entire crew.
details:
What it does / how it works: ASTRO combines astronauts' sleep-cycle data and short psychological scales into one personal-baseline well-being indicator on a dashboard, with alerts when warning patterns appear.

Benefits: It helps crews catch sleep and mental health changes early and gives astronauts simple, actionable information instead of raw data.

Intended impact: To support, not replace, flight surgeons and psychologists on long missions like Mars, and to help scientists on Earth understand psychological health in space.

Tools: Claude Ai

Creativity: Instead of treating sleep and mental well-being separately, ASTRO tracks how they change together for each astronaut against their own baseline.

Factors considered: Crew privacy and consent, personal baselines, circadian timing and light exposure, and clinical validation of thresholds.
